extracted.intended_audience: EPA rulemakers, regulated power industry stakeholders, environmental and energy policymakers, and public commenters on EPA NSPS rulemaking
extracted.subtask_short: evaluating CCS as BSER for coal EGUs
extracted.subtask_description: Assessment of whether carbon capture, transport, and sequestration (CCS) — particularly solvent/amine-based post-combustion capture achieving 90% CO2 removal — is adequately demonstrated, technically feasible, and achievable long-term for coal-fired steam generating units under EPA Section 111 rulemaking. The page documents demonstrations, vendor claims, operational lessons, and design/operational mitigation measures that support the EPA's BSER determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrated demonstration of CCS components
rubrics_metrics.description: All constituent components of CCS—carbon capture, transportation, and sequestration—have been demonstrated in integrated, simultaneous operation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The record includes examples (e.g., Great Plains Synfuels Plant transporting CO2 for storage and EOR; Boundary Dam Unit 3 and Petra Nova) that show capture, transport, and storage operating together. Even demonstrations of individual components would be sufficient if it is reasonable that they can function together because they have been engineered and designed to do so and are supported by decades of direct data and experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: CO2 capture efficiency — 90 percent standard
rubrics_metrics.description: The EPA is finalizing the determination that the CO2 capture component of CCS has been adequately demonstrated at a capture efficiency of 90 percent, is technically feasible, and is achievable over long periods (e.g., a year).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This determination is supported by commercial-scale installations (Boundary Dam Unit 3, Petra Nova), vendor guarantees, and identification of minor, currently available technological improvements that can be applied to ensure capture plants achieve 90 percent. Demonstrations that consistently treat the full flue gas (not only slipstreams) are relevant to assessing total plant-level capture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solvent-based (amine) post-combustion capture applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: Solvent-based (amine) capture has been the most widely demonstrated at commercial scale for post-combustion capture and is applicable to both combustion turbines and steam generating units.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Page cites numerous commercial and pilot projects using proprietary and non-proprietary amines (e.g., Shell CANSOLV®, MHI KS-1/KS-21™, Fluor Econamine FG Plus, BASF OASE® blue, ION solvents). Vendors report capture rates of 90% or higher and in some tests 95–99.8%. Use of proprietary solvents is common; non-proprietary solvents (e.g., MEA) exist. The technology description includes process flow: pretreatment → quencher → absorption column → solvent regeneration → compression → transport → solvent reclaiming.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pretreatment requirement — adequate SO2 and PM removal
rubrics_metrics.description: Adequate removal of SO2 and particulate matter (PM) prior to the CO2 capture system is necessary because amine solvents react with SO2 and PM can cause fouling and other operational problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preamble explains that PM and SO2 affect capture performance and provides examples of how fouling in upstream SO2 removal systems (e.g., at Boundary Dam) limited downstream CO2 capture. Conventional SO2 and PM controls (e.g., wet FGD, dry FGD, ESPs, baghouses, WESP) and additional wash/quench systems are recommended. The EPA accounts for costs of adding wet-FGD where absent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design and operational mitigations to address fouling and reliability issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Design improvements and operational practices (e.g., demister wash systems, pre-scrubber curtain spray, quencher throat sprays, booster fan wash, online cleaning of demisters, chemical cleans, replacement of fouled packing, redundancies and isolations of key heat exchangers, multiple compressor trains) are necessary and effective to mitigate fouling, scaling, foaming, and other operational challenges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boundary Dam and Petra Nova experiences are used as examples: retrofits and additions (wash systems, redundancy, gasket/material replacements, diversion walls, collection drains, filtering, compressor intercooler material replacement) corrected early operational problems. The preamble highlights routinely applied mitigations such as antifoam injection, solvent reclaiming, chemical shocking for biological fouling, and design choices that allow online maintenance. A feasibility study (Shand) showed such improvements at less cost than Boundary Dam.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational availability and maintenance expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Capture plants must demonstrate sufficient availability and be maintainable; historical availability metrics and outage patterns inform achievability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Petra Nova outages attributable to the capture facility decreased year-on-year and averaged less than 10% of the year; Boundary Dam reported 98.3% capture system availability in Q3 2023. Planned and unplanned outages are normal; regular maintenance and online-cleaning regimes mitigate fouling and improve availability. Record of decreasing outages and implemented fixes supports long-term achievability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vendor experience and commercial availability evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Technology providers' statements, operating histories, and performance guarantees demonstrating decades of experience and thousands of operating hours support that capture technologies are commercially available and can achieve ≥90% capture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vendors cited (Shell, MHI, Linde/BASF, Fluor, ION) claim long track records (some >30 years, some >50,000 operating hours), commercial deployments, and guarantees of bulk CO2 removal >90%. Vendor test results (e.g., KS-21 delivering 95–99.8% at TCM) and vendor descriptions of commercial readiness are used as evidence. Vendor assurances and operating histories are considered corroborating evidence in EPA's assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial-scale comparability and scalability
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstrations at commercial scale that treated flue gas with properties similar to affected sources corroborate that capture equipment and solvents work at commercial scale and can achieve capture rates of 90%.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petra Nova is cited because the flue gas properties (composition, temperature, pressure, density, flowrate) match similarly sized coal-fired units; Petra Nova captured 92.4% of the processed slipstream and sequestered most captured CO2 via EOR. Scaling and similarity of flue gas conditions are important to infer applicability to the target fleet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequestration component demonstration (EOR and geologic storage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Storage of captured CO2 via Enhanced Oil Recovery (EOR) and via geologic storage (deep saline aquifers) has been demonstrated for captured CO2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Great Plains Synfuels (transport to Weyburn/Midale for EOR), Boundary Dam storage in Aquistore deep saline aquifer, Petra Nova sequestering captured CO2 by EOR. EPA notes BSER is not premised on EOR; sequestration demonstrations include permanent geologic storage as well as EOR use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling variable loads, startups, and shutdowns — turndown capability
rubrics_metrics.description: Capture plants must be able to operate across variable loads; currently available technology provides turndown ratios (e.g., single capture train to ~50% throughput; two trains to ~25%) compatible with coal-fired units' turndown capabilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coal-fired steam generating units typically turndown to about 40% of maximum design capacity and have high duty cycles (average 70% in 2021). Historical turndown limits: Boundary Dam ~60% throughput, Petra Nova ~70% throughput. EPA concludes 50% turndown for a single capture train is achievable; two trains allow lower throughputs. This supports achievability across typical operating cycles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence from state requirements and policy recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: State laws, planning frameworks, and standards that require or incentivize CCS (often at 90% capture) provide corroborating evidence that CCS is established and effective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include Illinois Climate and Equitable Jobs Act requiring 90% capture for certain coal units, Michigan and California policy recognizing 90% capture as qualifying 'clean energy', and state strategic plans in Louisiana, Pennsylvania, North Dakota, Wyoming. State-level statutory and planning recognition is used as supporting evidence of industry deployment and policy acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of economic/regulatory incentives affecting operations
rubrics_metrics.description: Economic incentives and regulatory contexts can affect the fraction of flue gas treated (e.g., slipstream operation or bypass) and therefore total plant-level capture; such factors must be considered when evaluating demonstration evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boundary Dam operated with a portion (~25% average) of flue gas bypassing the capture plant for economic/regulatory reasons, reducing total plant-level capture even when slipstream capture efficiency was ~90%. EPA notes that increasing capture requirements and process optimizations can reduce bypass; economic incentives (e.g., 45Q tax credits, IRA) can make projects financially viable (e.g., Diamond Vault).
